mainTopic: Saying ה׳'s name in vain, כינויי כינויין for vows and oaths, and a new משנה on phrases that compare food to holy things
overview: The amud opens by finishing a ברייתא. A person dedicating a קרבן should say "קרבן" first and only then "לה׳", so that ה׳'s name is never left hanging for nothing. A קל וחומר then shows how serious it is to say ה׳'s name for no purpose at all. Next, the גמרא asks whether the argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש about כינויין matches an argument between בית שמאי and בית הלל about כינויי כינויין, substitutes for the substitutes. It gives two answers showing that the two arguments do not have to match. The גמרא then lists examples of כינויי כינויין for נדרים, חרם, נזירות and שבועה. It raises several unclear words that stay as questions (תיבעי), and brings שמואל's ruling that some look-alike words mean nothing. It also explains the משנה's word מוהי. Finally, a new משנה lists phrases that make food forbidden by comparing it to holy things, even without saying the word קרבן.

steps.title: Where do we learn not to say ה׳'s name before the word for the offering?
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא asks for a source that a person should not say "לה׳ עולה" or similar phrases, with ה׳'s name coming first.
steps.simpleTranslation: From where do we know that a person should not say "To ה׳ a burnt-offering," "To ה׳ a meal-offering," "To ה׳ a thanks-offering," or "To ה׳ a peace-offering"?
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא asks for a source for a rule about word order. When you dedicate a קרבן‎, ה׳'s name should not come first. This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Four common kinds of offerings are listed: עולה, מנחה, תודה and שלמים. In every example, ה׳'s name comes before the name of the offering. The ברייתא wants to know which פסוק tells us not to talk that way.

keyTerms.meaning: From where do we know? (asks for a source)
A burnt-offering, which is burned completely on the מזבח
A meal-offering, made of flour
A thanks-offering
Peace-offerings

phrases.english: From where do we know that a person should not say
"To ה׳ a burnt-offering," "To ה׳ a meal-offering,"
"To ה׳ a thanks-offering," "To ה׳ a peace-offering"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the ברייתא that the גמרא was quoting just before this section.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוק teaches that one should not put ה׳'s name before the name of the offering.

steps.title: The פסוק says "קרבן לה׳", with the offering first
steps.stepSummary: The source is the פסוק "קרבן לה׳", which puts the word for the offering before ה׳'s name.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק teaches us: "An offering to ה׳."
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא answers the question. The source is the פסוק "קרבן לה׳", where the word "קרבן" comes first and ה׳'s name comes second.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lesson comes from the order of the words in the פסוק. If you say "קרבן" first, ה׳'s name is only said once you have already committed to the dedication. If you say "לה׳" first, you might change your mind before finishing, and then ה׳'s name would have been said for nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: The פסוק teaches us (introduces the source)
An offering to ה׳‎ (ויקרא 1:2)

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a rule against dedicating offerings to ה׳. It is only about the order of the words: say "קרבן" first and ה׳'s name after it.

phrases.english: The verse teaches: "An offering to ה׳."
phrases.notes: ויקרא 1:2. Notice that the word for the offering comes before ה׳'s name.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 1.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The word order of the פסוק "קרבן לה׳" teaches that the offering is named first and ה׳'s name comes after.

steps.title: A קל וחומר: saying ה׳'s name for no reason is surely wrong
steps.stepSummary: If the תורה protects someone who is about to dedicate a קרבן from possibly saying ה׳'s name for nothing, then someone who says it for no purpose at all has certainly done wrong.
steps.simpleTranslation: And there is a קל וחומר: this person only meant to say ה׳'s name in connection with an offering, and still the תורה told him to say "An offering to ה׳." Then someone who says ה׳'s name for no purpose, how much more so!
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא builds a קל וחומר from the light case to the serious one. It goes from someone with a good purpose to someone who says ה׳'s name for no reason at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The person bringing a קרבן has a holy reason to say ה׳'s name. Even so, the תורה arranges his words so that the name will never be left hanging. Someone with no reason at all is far worse, so his act is certainly forbidden and serious.

keyTerms.meaning: A logical argument: if it is true in the lighter case, it is surely true in the more serious case
ה׳'s name
For nothing, in vain
How much more so

steps.whatToRemember: Say "קרבן" first and "לה׳" second, so that ה׳'s name is never said for nothing. Saying ה׳'s name for no purpose at all is certainly serious, as the קל וחומר shows.
steps.whyThisMatters: This ברייתא is a well-known source for how seriously we treat saying ה׳'s name in vain.

phrases.english: And it is a kal vachomer:
Just as this person, who did not intend

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא לְהַזְכִּיר שֵׁם שָׁמַיִם עַל הַקׇּרְבָּן —
phrases.english: anything except to mention ה׳'s name over an offering,
the Torah said "An offering to ה׳,"
then for nothing, how much more so!
phrases.notes: He means someone who says ה׳'s name for no purpose at all. That is surely forbidden.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְקַל וָחוֹמֶר: וּמָה זֶה שֶׁלֹּא נִתְכַּוֵּון
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Builds on the word-order rule from step 2 and applies it to a more serious case.
steps.raayaObject: Saying ה׳'s name for no purpose is seriously forbidden.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A קל וחומר from the word order of "קרבן לה׳" in the פסוק.

steps.title: Maybe this is an older argument: בית שמאי and בית הלל on substitutes for substitutes
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש matches an argument between בית שמאי and בית הלל about כינויי כינויין.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this is like an argument between תנאים? בית שמאי say: substitutes for the substitutes make things forbidden. And בית הלל say: substitutes for the substitutes leave things permitted.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא returns to the earlier argument about where כינויין come from. It brings an older argument between בית שמאי and בית הלל that might be the same argument. This step sets up the comparison, which the next step will explain.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier, רבי יוחנן said כינויין are words from other languages, and ריש לקיש said the חכמים made them up. Here the topic is a step further away: substitutes for the substitutes. בית שמאי say a vow made with them works and forbids the item. בית הלל say it does not work and the item stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say this is like an argument between תנאים?
Substitutes for the substitute words used for vows
Forbidden, meaning the vow works
Permitted, meaning the vow does not work

phrases.english: Shall we say it is like a dispute of Tannaim?
phrases.notes: "It" is the earlier argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש about where כינויין come from.

phrases.english: Substitutes for substitute terms make things forbidden.
Substitutes for substitute terms leave things permitted.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Leaves the ברייתא about word order and goes back to the earlier argument between רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש about כינויין.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: בית שמאי: a vow made with כינויי כינויין works. בית הלל: it does not work.

steps.title: Explaining the match: foreign words or words the חכמים made up?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that בית שמאי hold like רבי יוחנן (כינויין are foreign words) and בית הלל hold like ריש לקיש (the חכמים made them up).
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't it so that the one who says substitutes for substitutes are forbidden holds that substitutes are words from other languages? And the one who says they are permitted holds that they are words the חכמים made up?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out how each side of the older argument would line up with רבי יוחנן or ריש לקיש. It asks this as a question, and the answer is still coming.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Suppose כינויין are simply words from other languages. Then a substitute for them is also just another foreign word, so it should work too. That fits בית שמאי. Suppose instead the חכמים made up a set list of words. Then only the words they made up count, and substitutes for those words do not work. That fits בית הלל.

keyTerms.meaning: Isn't it so that? (introduces a suggested explanation)
He holds
Words from the languages of other nations
Words that the חכמים made up

steps.confusionAlert: This is only a suggestion phrased as a question ("isn't it so?"). The גמרא has not decided yet, and the answer comes next.

phrases.english: the one who says substitutes for substitutes are forbidden

phrases.notes: Some versions leave out the word in round brackets, so read it simply as "כינויין", the substitutes themselves.

phrases.english: are the language of other nations.
And the one who says they are permitted
holds it is language that the Sages made up?

steps.triggerLanguage: מַאי לָאו: מַאן דְּאָמַר כִּינּוּיֵי כִינּוּיִין אֲסוּרִין
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains how the argument of בית שמאי and בית הלל from step 4 would match רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether בית שמאי's view rests on the idea that כינויין are foreign words (like רבי יוחנן) and בית הלל's view rests on the idea that the חכמים made them up (like ריש לקיש).

steps.title: Everyone agrees substitute words are foreign language
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the suggested match. Everyone agrees that כינויין are foreign words. בית שמאי and בית הלל only argue about whether the nations also use the כינויי כינויין.
steps.simpleTranslation: No. Everyone agrees that substitute words come from the language of the nations. בית שמאי think the nations also speak using these further words. בית הלל think the nations do not speak using these words.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the idea from the last step that בית שמאי hold like רבי יוחנן and בית הלל hold like ריש לקיש. It shows that both of them could agree with רבי יוחנן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The argument is moved from a question of principle to a question of fact. Both sides agree that כינויין are real foreign words. The only question is whether the nations actually use the כינויי כינויין too. If they do, those words also count as a real way to make a vow.

keyTerms.meaning: Everyone agrees
Substitute words used in place of the main vow words
The language of the nations, meaning foreign words
They speak with, they use

steps.confusionAlert: Do not think בית הלל here agree with ריש לקיש, as step 5 suggested. In this answer, both בית שמאי and בית הלל agree with רבי יוחנן that כינויין are foreign words.

phrases.english: that substitute words are the language of the nations,
the nations also speak with these,
phrases.notes: "These" means the substitutes for the substitutes, the כינויי כינויין.

phrases.english: the nations do not speak with these.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the suggestion from step 5 that matches בית שמאי and בית הלל to רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proposed matching of the two arguments
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The argument between בית שמאי and בית הלל can be explained as a question of fact about how the nations speak, without connecting it to the argument of רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש.

steps.title: Second answer: the argument is about making a גזירה
steps.stepSummary: Another way to reject the match: בית שמאי make a גזירה on כינויי כינויין so people do not treat real כינויין lightly. בית הלל do not make such a גזירה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Or you can say: בית שמאי hold that we make a גזירה about substitutes of substitutes because of the real substitutes. בית הלל hold that we do not make a גזירה about substitutes of substitutes because of the real substitutes.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to explain the argument without linking it to רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here both sides agree that כינויי כינויין are not real words in any language. בית שמאי still treat them as a vow. They worry that otherwise people will start treating the real כינויין lightly too. בית הלל do not see a need for this extra protection.

keyTerms.meaning: And if you want, say (another answer)
We make a rabbinic גזירה as a protective rule
Substitutes for the substitute words

steps.whatToRemember: There are two ways to explain the argument between בית שמאי and בית הלל without linking it to רבי יוחנן and ריש לקיש. One is a question of fact: do the nations use these words? The other is a question of policy: should we make a גזירה?

phrases.english: we make a גזירה about substitutes of substitutes

phrases.notes: The worry is that if these don't count, people will start to take the real כינויין lightly too.

phrases.english: we do not make a גזירה about substitutes of substitutes

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives a second, different way to reject the match from step 5.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The proposed matching of the two arguments
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The argument can be about whether to make a protective גזירה, which has nothing to do with where the כינויין come from.

steps.title: What are substitutes of substitutes for vows?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for examples of כינויי כינויין for נדרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: What do substitutes of substitutes for vows look like?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for real examples of the words that בית שמאי and בית הלל argue about. This sets up a list of examples.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Up to now the discussion was about the general idea. Now the גמרא wants to know exactly which words count as כינויי כינויין, starting with נדרים.

keyTerms.meaning: What does it look like? What is the case?
Vows

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from explaining the argument to asking for actual examples of the words.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Examples of כינויי כינויין for נדרים

steps.title: רב יוסף's examples for vows
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף lists מקנמנא, מקנחנא, and מקנסנא as כינויי כינויין for נדרים.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב יוסף taught: "מקנמנא," "מקנחנא," "מקנסנא."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question with a ברייתא from רב יוסף that lists three words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These words are built from the כינויין קונם, קונח, and קונס that are in the משנה, turned into verb forms. Because they are one more step away from the original word, they are "substitutes of substitutes."

keyTerms.meaning: A common substitute word for קרבן in vows
A verb form of קונם, like "I make it קונם"

phrases.notes: These are verb forms of קונם, קונח, and קונס from the משנה.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question in step 8.

steps.title: Examples for חרם
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks about כינויי כינויין for חרם, and מפשאה lists חרקים, חרכים, and חרפים.
steps.simpleTranslation: What do substitutes of substitutes for חרם look like? מפשאה taught: "חרקים," "חרכים," "חרפים."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks the same question for חרם, a way of setting something aside for holy use, and answers it with examples.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This follows the same pattern as the list for vows. The examples are words that sound close to חרם but are changed even further.

keyTerms.meaning: Setting something aside as holy, or for the כהנים
Name of a חכם who taught ברייתות
A changed form of the word חרם

phrases.english: What do substitutes of substitutes for חרם look like?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Uses the same question and answer pattern as steps 8 and 9, now for חרם.

steps.title: Examples for נזירות
steps.stepSummary: רב יוסף lists מחזקנא, מנזחנא, and מפיחנא as כינויי כינויין for נזירות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Substitutes of substitutes for נזירות? רב יוסף taught: "מחזקנא," "מנזחנא," "מפיחנא."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its third group of examples, the words used for נזירות. The examples for שבועה come later, in step 16.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the third group of examples, after נדרים and חרם. The משנה's list also covers שבועות, and the גמרא gives the כינויי כינויין for שבועה later, in step 16.

keyTerms.meaning: Becoming a נזיר
A changed verb form connected to נזיר

steps.whatToRemember: The גמרא gives three examples each for נדרים, חרם, and נזירות, and later for שבועה. All of them are words that are one more step away from the כינויין in the משנה.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the list of examples that began in step 8.

steps.title: Unclear words: מיפחזנא, מיתחזנא, מיתעזנא
steps.stepSummary: The חכמים ask what the law is for three more words: מיפחזנא, מיתחזנא, and מיתעזנא. No answer is given.
steps.simpleTranslation: They asked: What about "מיפחזנא"? What about "מיתחזנא"? What about "מיתעזנא"?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא raises an איבעיא, a real open question, about three words that are not on the lists, and leaves it unanswered.
steps.deeperAnalysis: These words are even further from the known terms. So it is not clear whether they still count as a way of making a vow. The גמרא only asks the question here and does not settle it.

keyTerms.meaning: They asked (an open question)
What is the law?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the clear examples, asks about words whose status is unclear.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether מיפחזנא, מיתחזנא, and מיתעזנא count as words that make a vow

steps.title: רבינא asks about the word קינמא
steps.stepSummary: רבינא asks רב אשי whether קינמא means קונם, which would make a vow, or the spice cinnamon, which would not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבינא said to רב אשי: What about "קינמא"? Does he mean "קונם," or maybe he means "קנמן בשם," sweet cinnamon?
steps.whatsHappening: רבינא raises another unclear word. The question is whether the person meant a vow or was just naming a spice.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Unlike the last step, here the doubt is about what the person meant. The word קינמא sounds like קונם, but it also sounds like קנמן, the spice in the תורה. If he meant the spice, there is no vow at all.

keyTerms.meaning: An unclear word that could mean קונם or cinnamon
Or maybe
Sweet cinnamon, one of the spices in the anointing oil

steps.confusionAlert: The question is not whether קינמא is a weaker word for a vow. It is whether the person meant a vow at all, or was just naming a spice.

phrases.notes: Some versions have the word in round brackets and some don't; it is the same word repeated.

phrases.english: or maybe he is saying "sweet cinnamon"?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues asking about unclear words, now with a word that has two possible meanings.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether קינמא means קונם, which makes a vow, or the spice קנמן, which does not

steps.title: Does the word קינה mean a chicken coop or a vow?
steps.stepSummary: רב אחא בריה דרב חייא asks רב אשי whether the word קינה means a chicken coop or is a form of קונם.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב אחא son of רב חייא asked רב אשי: What about the word 'קינה'? Does he mean a chicken coop, or is it a way of saying 'קונם'?
steps.whatsHappening: Another unclear word is brought up. Like קינמא in the step before, the question is whether it is a vow word or just a normal word.
steps.deeperAnalysis: קינה is a real word for a chicken coop, so it may be harmless. But it also sounds very close to קונם, the classic vow word. The question is which meaning the speaker had in mind.

keyTerms.meaning: A chicken coop; also sounds like קונם
Chickens
Or maybe
A way of saying קונם

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב חִיָּיא
phrases.english: Rav Acha son of Rav Chiya said to him
Is he saying a coop of chickens,
or maybe it is a way of saying konam?

steps.triggerLanguage: אֲמַר לֵיהּ רַב אַחָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב חִיָּיא לְרַב אָשֵׁי: ״קִינָּה״ מַאי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Same kind of question as step 13 (קינמא), now about a different word.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Does the word קינה count as a vow word like קונם, or does it just mean a chicken coop?

steps.title: The questions stay unanswered
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא says תיבעי: these questions remain unsolved.
steps.simpleTranslation: It remains a question.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא closes the list of open questions and says no answer was found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: תיבעי means the question stays open. It seems to cover the open word questions just asked (steps 12–14), since none of them got an answer.

keyTerms.meaning: Let it stay a question; it is not solved

steps.whatToRemember: The words קינמא and קינה, and the questions just before them, stay as open questions.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the questions of steps 12–14 with no answer.

steps.title: Far-off nicknames for an oath
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the כינויי כינויין of שבועה are and lists שבואל, שבותיאל, and שקוקאל.
steps.simpleTranslation: What are the nicknames-of-nicknames for an oath? 'שבואל', 'שבותיאל', 'שקוקאל'.
steps.whatsHappening: After נדרים, חרם, and נזירות, the גמרא now gives the far-off nicknames for שבועה (an oath).
steps.deeperAnalysis: This copies the pattern of steps 9–11. These words are twisted forms of שבועה and שקוקה, so they may still work as an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: An oath
What does it look like? What are the cases?
A twisted form of שקוקה, a nickname for an oath

phrases.english: What are the nicknames-of-nicknames for an oath?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the list of כינויי כינויין, now for שבועה.

steps.title: שבואל is a person's name
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: שבואל is the name of שבואל בן גרשום, so it cannot be an oath word.
steps.simpleTranslation: שבואל? That means שבואל בן גרשום!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks one word on the list.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שבואל is a real person's name. Someone saying it would sound like he is naming a person, not taking an oath. So it does not belong on the list.

keyTerms.meaning: A person named in דברי הימים
It means; it sounds like

phrases.english: Shevuel? That means Shevuel son of Gershom!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the first word on the list in step 16.
steps.kashyaTarget: The word שבואל in the list of oath nicknames.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A word that is a known person's name sounds like a name, not like an oath.

steps.title: Fixing the list: שבובאל instead
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא fixes the list to שבובאל, שבותיאל, שקוקאל, and asks what their law is.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, the list is 'שבובאל', 'שבותיאל', 'שקוקאל'. What is the law?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא swaps שבואל for שבובאל, which is not anyone's name. Then it asks what the law is for these words.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Swapping the word removes the problem from step 17. The word מהו turns the list into a question, so it is not clear these words count. Next, שמואל rules on three other words that only sound a little like vow or oath words.

keyTerms.meaning: Rather; this fixes what was said before
The fixed word, which is not a person's name
What is the law?

steps.confusionAlert: Because of the word מהו, these words are now asked about. The גמרא is not saying for sure that they count.
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the objection of step 17 by changing the word.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Changing the wording of the list
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The list had שבואל, which is a person's name.
steps.terutzMaskana: The word is שבובאל, and the law for these words is asked about.

steps.title: שמואל: three words that mean nothing
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that אשיבתא, אשקיקא, and קרינשא do not make a vow or oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: If he said 'אשיבתא', he said nothing. 'אשקיקא', he said nothing. 'קרינשא', he said nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: שמואל names three words that sound a little like vow or oath words but have no power at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: אשיבתא and אשקיקא sound a bit like שבועה and שקוקה. קרינשא sounds a bit like קונם. Even so, they are too far away, so nothing happens.

keyTerms.meaning: He said nothing; no vow or oath happens
A word that sounds a little like שבועה
A word that sounds a little like קונם

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows there is a limit: a word that only slightly sounds like a vow word does not count.

phrases.english: If he said 'ashivta', he has said nothing,

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: אָמַר ״אַשִּׁיבְתָּא״ — לֹא אָמַר כְּלוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Comes right after the question מהו and gives a limit on oath and vow words.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: אשיבתא, אשקיקא, and קרינשא make no vow or oath.

steps.title: The word מוהי: only with 'an oath that מוהי said'
steps.stepSummary: On the משנה's word מוהי, רבן שמעון בן גמליאל teaches that 'במוהי' alone means nothing, but 'במומתא דאמר מוהי' is a nickname for an oath.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: 'If he vowed with מוהי, these are nicknames.' A ברייתא teaches: רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: One who says 'by מוהי' said nothing. 'By the oath that מוהי said' is a nickname for an oath.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא goes back to a line of the משנה about the word מוהי and brings a ברייתא that explains it.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Just saying 'by מוהי' is not enough. But if he says 'by the oath (מומתא) that מוהי said', the word מומתא clearly means an oath, so it works as a nickname for an oath.

keyTerms.meaning: A word from the משנה; alone it means nothing
An oath (Aramaic)

steps.whatToRemember: 'במוהי' alone does nothing; 'במומתא דאמר מוהי' is an oath nickname.

phrases.english: 'If he vowed with mohi, these are nicknames.'

phrases.aramaic: תַּנְיָא, רַבָּן שִׁמְעוֹן בֶּן גַּמְלִיאֵל אוֹמֵר:
phrases.english: It is taught: Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
One who says 'by mohi' has said nothing,
these are nicknames for an oath.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to the משנה and explains a new word, מוהי.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: מוהי alone means nothing; 'במומתא דאמר מוהי' is a nickname for an oath.

steps.title: New משנה: לחולין, not kosher, impure, נותר, פיגול
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that if someone calls food 'לחולין', 'not kosher', 'not pure', 'pure' and 'impure', or 'נותר' and 'פיגול', the food is forbidden to him.
steps.simpleTranslation: משנה: One who says, 'What I eat of yours is לחולין', or 'not kosher', 'not pure', 'pure', 'impure', 'נותר', or 'פיגול' — it is forbidden.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה starts. It lists phrases that make another person's food forbidden to the speaker.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'לחולין' is read as 'לא חולין', meaning 'not ordinary': the food is like holy food. 'נותר' and 'פיגול' are holy קרבנות that may not be eaten. Linking the food to these words makes it forbidden to him.

keyTerms.meaning: Read as 'לא חולין': not ordinary, so holy
Not pure (Aramaic)
Leftover meat of a קרבן past its time
A קרבן brought with the plan to eat it at the wrong time
Forbidden

steps.confusionAlert: 'לחולין' sounds like 'ordinary', but it is read as 'לא חולין', 'not ordinary', which is why the food becomes forbidden.

phrases.english: Mishnah: One who says, 'Lachullin is what I eat of yours',

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new משנה after the discussion of nicknames.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Calling another person's food לחולין, not kosher, not pure, pure and impure, נותר, or פיגול makes it forbidden to the speaker.

steps.title: More phrases that count as a vow by an offering
steps.stepSummary: The משנה continues its list: comparing food to the lamb, the pens, the altar's wood or fires, the מזבח, the היכל, or ירושלים, or to any altar item, makes a vow by קרבן even if the word קרבן was never said.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone says food is like the lamb, like the pens, like the wood, like the fires, like the altar, like the Sanctuary, or like Jerusalem, or if he vowed by any of the altar's utensils, even though he did not mention 'offering', it counts as a vow by an offering.
steps.whatsHappening: The משנה keeps going with its list of words that make food forbidden, now naming holy items connected to the מזבח and the מקדש.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The new idea is that you don't need the word קרבן itself. Comparing food to anything closely tied to offerings, like the altar or its wood and fire, is treated just like saying 'this is a קרבן to me', so the food becomes forbidden.

keyTerms.meaning: The lamb, meaning the lamb of the daily offering
Pens, where animals set aside as offerings were kept
The fires on the altar
The Sanctuary building in the בית המקדש
Things used in the altar's service
He made a vow by linking the item to an offering

steps.confusionAlert: The word 'like' (the letter כ at the start of each word) matters here. The person is not saying the food IS the altar, only that it should be treated like it. That comparison is what makes the vow work.
steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that a vow works through what the words point to, not only through saying the exact word קרבן.

phrases.english: Like the lamb, like the pens,
phrases.notes: The lamb is the daily offering. The pens held animals already set aside as offerings.

phrases.english: like the wood, like the fires,
phrases.notes: He means the wood and fires on the altar.

phrases.english: like the altar, like the Sanctuary, like Jerusalem.
If he vowed by any one of the utensils of the altar,

phrases.aramaic: אַף עַל פִּי שֶׁלֹּא הִזְכִּיר קׇרְבָּן
phrases.english: even though he did not mention 'offering'
this person has vowed by an offering.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues the משנה's list of vow phrases begun in step 21.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Comparing food to any item tied to the altar or the מקדש, or to an altar utensil, is a vow by קרבן even without saying the word קרבן.

steps.title: Saying just 'Jerusalem' means nothing
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהודה rules that someone who says 'ירושלים' without the word 'like' has said nothing, and no vow takes effect.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יהודה says: one who says 'Jerusalem' has not said anything.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יהודה adds a limit to the משנה's list: the bare word 'ירושלים', without 'like', does not make a vow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תנא קמא listed 'like ירושלים' (כירושלים) as a valid vow. רבי יהודה says that if the person drops the 'like' and just says 'ירושלים', the words don't connect the food to anything holy in a way that forbids it, so nothing happens.

keyTerms.meaning: He has said nothing; the words have no effect

steps.whatToRemember: The משנה lists many vow phrases tied to offerings and the מקדש. All work even without the word קרבן, but רבי יהודה says plain 'ירושלים' without 'like' is not a vow.
steps.triggerLanguage: רַבִּי יְהוּדָה אוֹמֵר: הָאוֹמֵר יְרוּשָׁלַיִם לֹא אָמַר כְּלוּם
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds a dissenting opinion limiting the phrase 'כירושלים' from step 22.
